reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: The commonest form of intestinal ischaemia, usually affecting older adults and typically arising from a transient, non-occlusive fall in colonic perfusion rather than a fixed arterial blockage
Classic presentation is sudden mild crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed within a day by the passage of bloody or maroon stool, with only modest blood loss
The watershed zones (splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction) are most vulnerable, while the rectum is usually spared because of its dual blood supply
CT often shows segmental bowel-wall thickening, and colonoscopy is the key diagnostic test showing segmental oedema, haemorrhage, and mucosal ulceration with an abrupt transition to normal mucosa
Most cases are non-gangrenous and settle with supportive care: bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and correction of any precipitating hypoperfusion
Right-sided (isolated right colon) involvement carries a worse prognosis and should raise concern for coexisting acute mesenteric ischaemia
Distinguish from infective colitis and inflammatory bowel disease; the segmental distribution and rapid resolution favour an ischaemic cause
Recognised triggers include hypotension, cardiac or vascular surgery, dehydration, hypercoagulable states, and certain drugs such as vasoconstrictors
reference.pathophysiology: Ischaemic colitis results from a temporary reduction in blood flow to a colonic segment, most often a low-flow (non-occlusive) event superimposed on the marginal circulation of watershed areas. Reduced perfusion injures the mucosa first, producing oedema, submucosal haemorrhage, and superficial ulceration. In most patients reperfusion allows healing, but persistent or severe ischaemia can progress to transmural (gangrenous) necrosis with perforation or, later, to fibrotic stricture. It is usually a disease of small vessels and systemic hypoperfusion rather than a large-artery occlusion, which distinguishes it from acute mesenteric ischaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn colitis
additionalInvestigations: CT of the abdomen and pelvis to assess segmental wall thickening and exclude perforation
Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy showing segmental mucosal injury with an abrupt transition zone
Serum lactate and inflammatory markers to gauge severity and detect possible gangrene
Stool studies to exclude infective causes when the picture is atypical
Cardiac and vascular assessment to identify a precipitating low-flow state
redFlags: Peritonism, fever, marked leucocytosis, or rising lactate suggesting gangrenous colitis and impending perforation
Isolated right-sided colonic involvement, which may signal concurrent acute mesenteric ischaemia
Persistent bleeding, haemodynamic instability, or failure to improve on supportive care
Development of a colonic stricture with obstruction during recovery
reference.prognosis: Non-gangrenous ischaemic colitis usually resolves within a few days with conservative management and has a good outcome. Gangrenous disease requiring surgery carries substantial mortality, and right-sided involvement predicts a worse course. A minority develop chronic segmental colitis or a stricture.
pitfalls: Assuming rectal sparing excludes colonic ischaemia, or mistaking segmental ischaemic changes for inflammatory bowel disease
Delaying surgical review when signs of transmural necrosis are present
Overlooking a precipitating hypoperfusion event that will otherwise recur
Failing to recognise that isolated right colon disease may reflect small-bowel mesenteric ischaemia needing urgent vascular evaluation
management: Treat most non-gangrenous cases conservatively with bowel rest, intravenous fluid resuscitation and correction of the precipitating hypoperfusion
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics in moderate-to-severe disease
Optimise the circulation and review offending vasoconstrictor or precipitating medications
Proceed urgently to surgical resection for gangrenous, fulminant or perforated colitis, and hold heightened concern for coexisting acute mesenteric ischaemia in isolated right-colon disease
Monitor with serial examination and lactate and inflammatory markers to detect transmural progression
Identify and address an underlying cardiac, vascular or thrombophilic low-flow cause
Follow up for the development of chronic segmental colitis or a fibrotic stricture requiring later intervention
